metadata.title: Microsoft's Green Card Filings Reveal A Striking Pattern After Mass Layoffs. Trump's New Rule Could Freeze Sponsorships For Two Years.

content.text:
Microsoft nearly stopped filing employment-based green card applications following its 2025 layoffs, submitting just 23 applications over the next 11 months, according to an analysis of federal labor records shared with International Business Times. The findings come as the Trump administration proposes a two-year restriction that could make it substantially harder for technology companies to sponsor foreign workers after certain layoffs.
The analysis also revealed another striking pattern: Microsoft disclosed layoffs in 86% of its Permanent Labor Certification, or PERM, applications decided by the Department of Labor in fiscal 2026, up from 79% the previous year.
The figures were compiled by Adam Ali, co-founder and data analyst at PERM Tracker, which examines publicly available Department of Labor records. Ali provided IBT with employer-level data, filing histories and additional analysis of Microsoft's immigration sponsorship patterns.
Of Microsoft's 1,722 PERM applications decided between October 2025 and September 2026, 1,474 answered yes to a question asking whether the employer had laid off workers in the relevant occupation and geographic area during the six months before filing.
In fiscal 2025, Microsoft reported qualifying layoffs in 2,493 of its 3,158 decided applications.
The disclosures do not establish that Microsoft replaced laid-off American workers with foreign employees or violated immigration regulations. The records reflect employers' answers about layoffs in occupations and locations connected to individual applications, many of which were filed well before the year in which they were decided.
Nevertheless, the findings provide a detailed picture of how one of America's largest technology companies managed its green card sponsorship filings through successive rounds of workforce reductions.
Under existing rules, employers can continue seeking PERM certification after qualifying layoffs if they meet requirements to notify and consider potentially qualified U.S. workers for the available positions.
That could change under a Labor Department proposal published Nov. 17. The proposed regulation would generally prevent an employer from filing a permanent labor certification application if it laid off U.S. workers in the same or a similar occupation and geographic area during the preceding two years.
The restriction would apply to qualifying layoffs rather than automatically blocking every green card application at a company that reduced its workforce.
Microsoft's filing history illustrates why the distinction matters. The company submitted 512 PERM applications in January 2023 before filing activity fell sharply during layoffs in Washington state, according to Ali's analysis of Labor Department records and state layoff notices.
Microsoft subsequently resumed filing in larger numbers, submitting 675 applications in November 2023, approximately two months after its last reported Washington layoffs of that year took effect.
Many applications filed during that period disclosed layoffs within the preceding six months.
The company's response to its 2025 workforce reductions was different. Microsoft submitted 451 PERM applications in May 2025, then filed just 23 over the following 11 months.
Its filing activity resumed in May 2026, when the company submitted 247 applications, about six months after its last reported Washington state layoff of 2025 took effect.
"DOL's files show both choices today's six-month rule allows after a layoff. After Microsoft's 2023 layoffs, the company went back to filing early and told DOL about the layoffs on its applications. After its 2025 layoffs, Microsoft waited six months before filing again," Ali told International Business Times.
The records show when applications were filed and whether employers disclosed layoffs. They do not establish why Microsoft changed its filing strategy.
Microsoft did not respond to requests for comment, including a follow-up, about the findings or the potential impact of the proposed restrictions.
The data also reveals how significantly disclosure rates varied across occupations. In fiscal 2025, Microsoft reported relevant layoffs in 2,041 of its 2,254 applications for software developers, compared with 47 of 177 applications for data scientists.
Location also made a difference. Among Microsoft's applications involving Washington state worksites, 88% disclosed qualifying layoffs, compared with 23% elsewhere, PERM Tracker found.
These differences are particularly relevant because the proposed restriction would depend on the occupation and location involved, not simply whether an employer had conducted layoffs somewhere in the country.
Sabrina Soltau, an immigration attorney, told International Business Times that the current system allows employers to proceed after layoffs if they satisfy the Labor Department's recruitment and worker-protection requirements.
The proposed rule would impose a substantially longer restriction on employers that laid off U.S. workers in the same or a similar occupation in the relevant geographic area.
For example, a company that laid off software developers in Seattle could be prevented from filing a PERM application for a comparable position there for two years.
It could still potentially sponsor an employee for an unrelated occupation or at another location where no qualifying layoff had occurred.
The consequences could be particularly serious for foreign workers approaching the limits of their temporary immigration status.
H-1B workers generally face a six-year limit, although employees who reach certain milestones in the employment-based green card process may qualify for extensions.
A two-year restriction could delay the filing of a labor certification application long enough to create problems for workers who have already spent several years in the United States.
"A two-year bar on filing on top of that could leave a worker four or five years into H-1B status with nothing filed in time," Soltau said.
Workers who already have approved immigrant petitions may have additional extension options, meaning the impact would vary depending on the stage of each person's immigration process.
The proposed regulation would also introduce requirements for employers that lay off U.S. workers after filing a labor certification application but before the associated immigrant petition is resolved.
In qualifying cases, employers would have to report the layoffs within five business days and offer the sponsored position to affected U.S. workers, subject to the proposal's conditions.
The proposed rule comes as Microsoft is already facing a separate government restriction on its green card sponsorship program.
On Oct. 8, the Trump administration suspended Microsoft, Adobe and six major IT services companies from the PERM program, citing federal investigations into potential immigration-related violations.
Vice President JD Vance and Labor Department officials announced that the government would stop accepting or processing PERM applications involving the affected companies.
According to PERM Tracker's monitoring of Labor Department case-status records, 598 Microsoft applications were listed as on hold following the suspension.
The October suspension and the proposed two-year layoff restriction are separate government actions. The Labor Department has not publicly established that Microsoft's layoff disclosures caused the suspension.
The broader federal data also shows that reporting layoffs has not historically prevented most PERM applications from receiving certification.
Of 6,807 applications decided in fiscal 2025 that disclosed relevant layoffs, 6,408 were certified, according to Ali's analysis.
Microsoft received certifications for 2,296 of its 2,493 applications that disclosed layoffs that year, while eight were denied and 189 were withdrawn.
"Answering yes to the PERM form's layoff question is a disclosure, and DOL certified 94% of those applications last year, the same rate as the applications that answered no," Ali said.
"The proposal would turn a layoff into a two-year bar. Today's data can't show how many applications that would stop, because today's form asks about six months and related jobs, while the bar would cover two years and the same or a similar job."
The findings are based on employers' answers in the Labor Department's public PERM disclosure files, including the field identifying whether relevant layoffs occurred before an application was filed.
PERM Tracker counted applications by fiscal year of decision, included cases classified as certified or certified-expired in certification totals, and analyzed filing dates separately to identify changes in company activity.
The records do not contain the number of workers affected by each reported layoff, and they cannot establish how many applications would be prohibited under the proposed two-year restriction.
The Labor Department has similarly acknowledged that the impact of the proposed change cannot be reliably quantified using available information.
Public comments on the regulation remain open until Jan. 19, 2027.
